judge_input.description:
<!-- Each and every single pull request must be associated right together with some open issue of its own, unless of course it just so happens to be the particular case that the request in question is a documentation fix. In the event that it turns out that a corresponding issue does not already happen to exist anywhere, then please do go right ahead and take the time to create one for it, so that we are all able to properly discuss the change together first before anything else. -->

<!-- Please do take a moment of your time to go ahead and answer each of the following questions below. We do, as a matter of standing policy, end up closing any and all of the pull requests that happen to not answer them at all. -->

> Which issue, if any, is this issue related to?

Similar to https://github.com/stylelint/stylelint/pull/9061

> Is there anything in the PR that needs further explanation?

This particular PR right here goes right ahead and changes the rule in such a way that it is now going to only ever go and call `fork` in one of two specific situations: the first is if the `*syntax` secondary options happen to be the ones that are actually being used, and the second is if the file that happens to be getting linted contains within it some `@property` at-rules that go on to extend the syntax. In any and every other case at all besides just those two particular ones, the rule will instead simply go and make use of the cached lexer that it is able to get for itself from out of `context`.

I am, at some point soon, going to go ahead and open up a separate issue specifically in order to remove those secondary options entirely and completely (they are, as of this point in time, now genuinely redundant, and this is on account of the plain fact that we went and added in `languageOption` earlier), and the whole goal behind doing that is so that only the more performant `languageOption` is the one single thing that ends up remaining available going forward. That all said, it does nonetheless seem to genuinely be the case that the forking on any brand new definitions that appear within a file is simply something that turns out to be entirely unavoidable, though.

This was all benchmarked, and it was done so by making use of our own standard config, which is the following:

```
export default {
	extends: ['stylelint-config-standard'],
};
```

The upshot of it is that it goes on to very nearly halve the total amount of time that it ends up taking whenever running our config across a full set of 1000 separate CSS files:

```
# Before
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Size      Files   Rules   Overrides   Time        ±CV     Per file  Memory      
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Small     20      0       0           247.03ms    2.2%    12.35ms   201.36 MB   
  Medium    100     0       0           701.05ms    1.2%    7.01ms    438.20 MB   
  Large     500     0       0           2.82s       1.4%    5.63ms    471.03 MB   
  X-Large   1000    0       0           5.45s       0.2%    5.45ms    575.78 MB   
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# After
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Size      Files   Rules   Overrides   Time        ±CV     Per file  Memory      
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Small     20      0       0           192.60ms    2.2%    9.63ms    163.20 MB   
  Medium    100     0       0           436.75ms    1.1%    4.37ms    272.27 MB   
  Large     500     0       0           1.58s       0.5%    3.15ms    448.00 MB   
  X-Large   1000    0       0           2.95s       0.5%    2.95ms    604.58 MB   
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# Comparison

 Size      Baseline    Current     Diff        Change    Status    
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Small     247.03ms    192.60ms    54.43ms     -22.0%    ✓ Faster  
  Medium    701.05ms    436.75ms    264.30ms    -37.7%    ✓ Faster  
  Large     2.82s       1.58s       1.24s       -44.1%    ✓ Faster  
  X-Large   5.45s       2.95s       2.50s       -45.8%    ✓ Faster  
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

And then, on top of all of that, the cumulative gains that you get once this is combined right together with https://github.com/stylelint/stylelint/pull/9061 are as follows:

```
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  PERFORMANCE COMPARISON
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Size      Baseline    Current     Diff        Change    Status    
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Small     247.03ms    147.65ms    99.38ms     -40.2%    ✓ Faster  
  Medium    701.05ms    273.86ms    427.19ms    -60.9%    ✓ Faster  
  Large     2.82s       823.33ms    1.99s       -70.8%    ✓ Faster  
  X-Large   5.45s       1.33s       4.12s       -75.6%    ✓ Faster  
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

To restate the essence of the whole change in plainer terms: what it really comes down to is that the rule now goes out of its way to avoid making the relatively expensive `fork` call in the common, everyday case, and it only ever ends up paying that particular cost in those specific situations where either the `*syntax` secondary options or else the `@property` at-rules genuinely make it necessary to do so; in every other case, it simply goes and reuses the cached lexer that it already has on hand from `context`. And it is precisely this one change in behavior which is what ends up directly producing all of the large and substantial speed-ups that can be seen laid out in the benchmark numbers up above. The before-and-after tables make the effect quite clear: across the small, medium, large, and extra-large sizes, the time taken drops considerably, and the comparison table confirms that every single one of those sizes ends up faster than it was before, with the improvements only growing larger still once the gains are combined together with those coming from the related pull request.

It is worth dwelling on the benchmark methodology just a little bit more, purely for the sake of being thorough about it. The whole set of measurements was carried out by making use of our own standard config, the very same one that is shown up above, and the runs themselves were carried out across four distinct sizes of workload: a Small one of 20 files, a Medium one of 100 files, a Large one of 500 files, and finally an X-Large one of a full 1000 files. In the very first of the tables, labelled as the Before table, you can see the timings exactly as they stood beforehand, prior to any of this change having been applied at all. Then, in the second of the tables, the one that is labelled as the After table, you can go and see those very same timings again, but now as they stand once the change here has actually been put into place. And then, in the third table, the Comparison one, the two sets of figures are placed directly side by side against one another, together with the raw difference between them and the percentage change, and every single row of it ends up being marked clearly as being faster than it was before. The final table, the cumulative PERFORMANCE COMPARISON one, then goes on to show what happens once these particular gains are stacked together on top of the gains that come from the closely related pull request, and, as you can plainly see there, the resulting improvements end up being larger still, ranging all the way from a reduction of around forty percent at the small end right up to a reduction of over seventy-five percent at the very largest end of the scale.
judge_input.title: Fix `declaration-property-value-no-unknown` performance
